results.title: Aldehydes in Alcohol-Induced Organ Injury
results.abstract:
Project Summary
Long-term heavy drinking causes multiple organ injury with the liver as the most impacted organ. Alcoholic liver
disease (ALD) covers a spectrum of liver lesions, including simple steatosis, alcoholic hepatitis and cirrhosis.
Unfortunately, FDA approved medication is not available for any stage of ALD. Thus, there is an urgent need to
investigate the mechanisms of disease pathogenesis and explore therapeutic strategies for ALD. Increasing
evidence support that translocation of pathogen associated molecular patterns (PAMP) from the intestine to
the liver triggers hepatic inflammation. During the past funding period, we investigated the role of type 1
conventional dendritic cells (cDC1s) in alcohol-induced defects at the gut-liver axis. We observed that Chronic
alcohol feeding reduced intestinal cDC1s and IL-12. In accordance, Th1 cells and their INF- expression were
also reduced. Batf3 knockout mice (cDC1 deficient) showed that cDC1 deficiency exaggerated alcohol-
reduced Th1/IFN- and worsened alcohol-induced dysbiosis, gut barrier dysfunction, PAMP translocation and
hepatic inflammation. Adaptive transfer of cDC1s reversed alcohol-decreased intestinal defects and
amelioration of ALD. We also found that IFN-γ administration restored intestinal STAT1 and STAT3,
upregulated AMPs, orchestrated gut microbiota, and reversed alcohol-induced endotoxemia and hepatic
inflammation. These results suggest that dysregulation of dendritic cell-T cell axis represents a novel
mechanism in alcohol-induced pathogenesis at the gut-liver axis. Our preliminary studies further demonstrated
that chronic alcohol feeding increased type 2 conventional dendritic cells (cDC2s) in the intestine, suggesting
an imbalance between cDC1 and cDC2 responses. cDC2s after antigen acquisition in the lamina propria
migrate to lymph tissues and induce Th17 cell differentiation. Indeed, we observed that CD4+IL-17+ T cells
(Th17 cells) were increased in the lymph tissues after alcohol exposure. We also found that alcohol increased
the dendritic cell surface succinate receptor, GPR91, in association with increased intestinal succinate. These
results suggest a novel host immunity-microbiota crosstalk mechanism in activation of cDC2s-Th17 cells circuit
in alcohol-induced pathogenesis at the gut-liver axis. This renewal project plans to investigate the role of DC2
activation and induction of Th17 response and the mechanism of how alcohol activate cDC2s in the
pathogenesis of ALD. The project will carry out three aims. Aim 1 is to determine the causal role of intestinal
cDC2 cell activation in alcohol-induced pathogenesis at the gut-liver axis. Aim 2 is to investigate a succinate-
activated GPR91 signaling pathway in alcohol-induced intestinal DC2 activation and migration. Aim 3 is to
determine the mechanisms by which alcohol elicits an intestinal succinate signal.

results.title: Ion Channels and Membrane Receptors in Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension
results.abstract:
PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT
Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a fatal and progressive disease with unknown etiology and poor
survival rate. Pulmonary vasoconstriction, vascular remodeling and occlusive intimal lesion are the major causes
for the elevated pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) in PAH. A rise in cytosolic Ca2+ concentration ([Ca2+]cyt) is
a trigger for pulmonary arterial smooth muscle cell (PASMC) contraction (and vasoconstriction) and a stimulus
for PASMC proliferation/migration (and vascular remodeling). In addition, the contractile-to-proliferative
phenotypic transition (CPPT) in PASMC and endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EndMT) in pulmonary
arterial endothelial cells (PAEC) are implicated in the development of pulmonary vascular remodeling and
obliterative intimal lesion in PAH. We recently found that Piezo1, a mechanosensitive cation channel, and
CALHM1 (calcium homeostasis modulator 1), a voltage-gated cation and ATP channel, are upregulated during
CPPT and involved in vascular remodeling in PAH/PH. Upregulated Piezo1 in PAEC enhances EndMT via the
Ca2+/AKT/mTOR-Jagged1 (Jag-1) signaling axis and is involved in the development of occlusive vascular lesion
and concentric vascular remodeling in animals with experimental pulmonary hypertension (PH). In addition, we
identified GPR91 (a succinate-activated GPCR) and GPR68 (a mechanosensitive GPCR) that are involved in
the development of pulmonary vascular remodeling in PAH/PH. The central hypothesis is that ionic (channel)
remodeling is required for phenotypic transition of PASMC/PAEC. Upregulated channels (Piezo1/CALHM1) and
receptors (GPR68/91) are required for causing pathogenic overgrowth of PASMC/EC through activation of Ca2+-
sensitive signaling and compartmentation of AKT/mTORC1 signaling, and contribute to vascular remodeling and
occlusive intimal lesion in PAH. The overall goals of this study are to examine: 1) gene expression profile
associated with the phenotypic transition of PASMC (CPPT) and PAEC (EndMT), 2) cellular and molecular
mechanisms involved in CPPT in human PASMC, 3) whether Piezo1 and mechanosensitive Ca2+ signaling
contribute to inducing and regulating EndMT in PAEC and whether endothelial Piezo1 is involved in the
development of PH, 4) how compartmentalized AKT/mTORC1 signaling and spatiotemporal Ca2+ signaling are
involved in EndMT in PAEC and enhanced PAEC proliferation in PAH/PH, 5) whether viroporins (e.g., SARS-
CoV-2 E protein) form non-selective cation channels to promote Ca2+ influx and stimulate PASMC/EC
proliferation, and 6) whether and how Ca2+ influx through upregulated cation channels and activation of selected
receptors contribute to regulation of inflammasome in PASMC/EC. The importance of this research program is
in its integrative design and translational potential in which we will define the pathogenic mechanism, identify
new therapeutic targets, and develop novel therapies for PAH/PH based on our studies on mechanosensitive
channels/receptors and Ca2+ signaling in PASMC and PAEC.

results.title: Ion Channels and Membrane Receptors in Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension
results.abstract:
PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT
Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a fatal and progressive disease with unknown etiology and poor
survival rate. Pulmonary vasoconstriction, vascular remodeling and occlusive intimal lesion are the major causes
for the elevated pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) in PAH. A rise in cytosolic Ca2+ concentration ([Ca2+]cyt) is
a trigger for pulmonary arterial smooth muscle cell (PASMC) contraction (and vasoconstriction) and a stimulus
for PASMC proliferation/migration (and vascular remodeling). In addition, the contractile-to-proliferative
phenotypic transition (CPPT) in PASMC and endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EndMT) in pulmonary
arterial endothelial cells (PAEC) are implicated in the development of pulmonary vascular remodeling and
obliterative intimal lesion in PAH. We recently found that Piezo1, a mechanosensitive cation channel, and
CALHM1 (calcium homeostasis modulator 1), a voltage-gated cation and ATP channel, are upregulated during
CPPT and involved in vascular remodeling in PAH/PH. Upregulated Piezo1 in PAEC enhances EndMT via the
Ca2+/AKT/mTOR-Jagged1 (Jag-1) signaling axis and is involved in the development of occlusive vascular lesion
and concentric vascular remodeling in animals with experimental pulmonary hypertension (PH). In addition, we
identified GPR91 (a succinate-activated GPCR) and GPR68 (a mechanosensitive GPCR) that are involved in
the development of pulmonary vascular remodeling in PAH/PH. The central hypothesis is that ionic (channel)
remodeling is required for phenotypic transition of PASMC/PAEC. Upregulated channels (Piezo1/CALHM1) and
receptors (GPR68/91) are required for causing pathogenic overgrowth of PASMC/EC through activation of Ca2+-
sensitive signaling and compartmentation of AKT/mTORC1 signaling, and contribute to vascular remodeling and
occlusive intimal lesion in PAH. The overall goals of this study are to examine: 1) gene expression profile
associated with the phenotypic transition of PASMC (CPPT) and PAEC (EndMT), 2) cellular and molecular
mechanisms involved in CPPT in human PASMC, 3) whether Piezo1 and mechanosensitive Ca2+ signaling
contribute to inducing and regulating EndMT in PAEC and whether endothelial Piezo1 is involved in the
development of PH, 4) how compartmentalized AKT/mTORC1 signaling and spatiotemporal Ca2+ signaling are
involved in EndMT in PAEC and enhanced PAEC proliferation in PAH/PH, 5) whether viroporins (e.g., SARS-
CoV-2 E protein) form non-selective cation channels to promote Ca2+ influx and stimulate PASMC/EC
proliferation, and 6) whether and how Ca2+ influx through upregulated cation channels and activation of selected
receptors contribute to regulation of inflammasome in PASMC/EC. The importance of this research program is
in its integrative design and translational potential in which we will define the pathogenic mechanism, identify
new therapeutic targets, and develop novel therapies for PAH/PH based on our studies on mechanosensitive
channels/receptors and Ca2+ signaling in PASMC and PAEC.

results.abstract:
Project Summary
Long-term heavy drinking causes multiple organ injury with the liver as the most impacted organ. Alcoholic liver
disease (ALD) covers a spectrum of liver lesions, including simple steatosis, alcoholic hepatitis and cirrhosis.

results.title: New CRISPR-based technologies for screening dark GPCRs
results.abstract:
PROJECT SUMMARY
Non-olfactory G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are the largest and most therapeutically targeted
class of cell surface receptors in humans. However, only a fraction (30% or 134) are currently drug targets.
Given the importance of GPCRs in human health, the large number of remaining understudied (i.e. “dark”)
GPCRs hold great potential for therapeutic development. For this proposal we have selected three dark
GPCRs (Gpr4, Gpr87, and Gpr91) from the list of 102 receptors organized by the Illuminating the
Druggable Genome (IDG) program. Our goal is to use these GPCRs to develop technologies (Aim 1)
and methods (Aim 2) that could be used to study many other IDG-eligible receptor targets in the future.
In Aim 1, we would pilot our new CRISPR-based technology, called PAM-scanning, to build hundreds of
dark GPCR-lysozyme chimeras in preparation for structural studies. PAM-scanning is made possible by
several other new techniques we are developing in our lab, including a new yeast-based GPCR screening
platform that we would optimize in Aim 2 for dark GPCR drug discovery. These two aims would address
three specific criteria requested in the FOA: preparing dark GPCRs for structure determination,
establishing preliminary structure-activity relationships against libraries of GPCR bioactive compounds,
and optimizing an assay (for drug screening in this case) for further investigations of other dark receptors.
Our choice to focus on Gpr4, Gpr87, and Gpr91 is based on several important factors: none are listed on
IDG’s protein illumination timeline, all express in our assay system and respond to their reported ligands,
and each is a promising therapeutic target for diseases like cancer (Gpr4 & Gpr87) and diabetes (Gpr91).
Support for this proposal would help us establish structure-based drug discovery campaigns for these
three dark receptors, and would generate new technologies for GPCR structure determination (Aim 1)
and drug discovery (Aim 2) that could be applied to other GPCR targets of interest to the IDG program.

results.title: Renin activation in early diabetes
results.abstract: DESCRIPTION (provided by applicant):  The incidence of diabetes mellitus and obesity are rapidly rising to epidemic levels in the United States and worldwide. Hyperglycemia, the metabolic hallmark of diabetes is a significant causative factor for the complications of diabetes mellitus, which results in significant morbidity and mortality for millions of Americans. Hyperglycemia is clearly associated with microvascular complications in many organs including the kidney, and diabetic nephropathy is the leading cause of end-stage renal disease (ESRD) in developed countries. In addition, diabetes may lead to macrovascular complications and systemic hypertension. Recent advances on the cellular and kidney-specific effects of hyperglycemia places the activation of the local, intra-renal renin-angiotensin system (RAS) as a strong candidate for the core abnormality that leads to other biochemical and cellular defects and the resulting renal tissue injury. Renin release from juxtaglomerular cells is the rate-limiting step of RAS activation. Novel discovery of the G-protein-coupled receptor GPR91, activated by citric acid cycle intermediate succinate, may provide a link between glucose metabolism and renin-dependent increases in blood pressure. We have recently established an imaging technique in which renin content, release, and tissue activity can be directly visualized in the intact living kidney tissue. The broad, long-term objective of this application is to establish that hyperglycemia in early diabetes causes the activation of the newly identified, kidney-specific metabolic receptor GPR91 which in turn initiates paracrine signaling and triggers renin release and glomerular hyperfiltration. Specific aims of this grant are to identify the cell types and molecules involved in succinate signaling, establish the mechanism of high glucose-induced renin release in vitro, and test the importance of GPR91/renin in the development of diabetic complications in vivo. Primary cell cultures, the isolated, in vitro microperfused afferent arteriole-glomerulus preparation, and in vivo mouse and rat kidney animal models will be used in combination with multi-photon fluorescence microscopy, and real-time imaging. These studies should yield clinically important information that can be used to develop new drugs and therapeutic approaches for the better treatment of diabetic complications in the kidney as well as high blood pressure.

results.title: Illumination of TAAR2 Location, Function and Regulators
results.abstract:
Project Summary
This proposal is prepared in response to RFA-RM-22-024, which invites “Pilot projects investigating
understudied G protein-coupled receptors, ion channels and protein kinases”. We choose to study trace amine
associated receptor 2 (TAAR2) which is an understudied GPCR and an IDG-eligible protein under this FOA.
TAAR2 was discovered as a GPCR in 2001 and has been speculated to be involved in neurological and
psychiatric diseases; however, little progress has been made towards understanding the action of TAAR2 and
creating experimental tools. To address the current knowledge gap, we will investigate TAAR2 cellular and
subcellular localization, trafficking and signal transduction using human SH-SY5Y cells and rodent brains.
Further, this proposal will also apply CRISPR/Cas9-mediated homology-directed repair mechanism to tag
Taar2 gene in SH-SY5Y cells so that TAAR2-interacting protein network can be revealed through proteomics.
Knowledge learned and products generated from this proposal will add value to the IDG program and
importantly, lay ground work for future investigation of TAAR2 in animal models of human diseases.

results.title: Mechanisms Underlying TAAR1-induced Wakefulness and REM Sleep Suppression
results.abstract:
PROJECT SUMMARY
 Trace amine-associated receptor 1 (TAAR1) is a G protein-coupled receptor involved in the regulation of
dopaminergic, serotonergic and glutamatergic activity. TAAR1 agonists have anxiolytic, antidepressant-, and
antipsychotic-like properties in both rodent and non-human primates; TAAR1 agonists are in clinical trials for
schizophrenia and Parkinson’s disease psychosis. We have previously shown that TAAR1 agonists are wake-
promoting in mice, rats and, most recently, non-human primates, characterized the sleep/wake phenotype of
Taar1 knockout (KO) and overexpressing (OE) mice, and evaluated the effects of TAAR1 agonists on
sleep/wake in wildtype (WT), KO and OE mice. We also showed that two different TAAR1 agonists suppressed
REM sleep and reduced cataplexy in mouse models of narcolepsy, precisely the properties desirable in a
narcolepsy therapeutic. Having established TAAR1 agonists as potential novel treatments for narcolepsy, we
will now investigate the underlying in vivo neurobiology. In Taar1-LacZ mice, we will determine whether TAAR1
is expressed in monoaminergic, glutamatergic or other cell types and use the RNAscope technology to
determine endogenous Taar1 mRNA expression in WT and KO mice and rats. Since TAAR1 negatively
regulates dopaminergic (DA) neuronal activity in vitro, we will test the hypothesis that TAAR1 partial agonism
promotes wakefulness by modulating DA arousal systems. To address this hypothesis, we will assess
neuronal activity in the ventral tegmental area and dorsal raphe nuclei of DAT-ires-Cre mice using in vivo Ca2+
microendoscopy, and determine whether pretreatment with DA D1- and D2-receptor antagonists attenuates
TAAR1-mediated wake-promotion. Since serotonergic neurons are wake-active and REM-inactive and TAAR1
negatively regulates serotonergic neuronal activity in vitro, we will also test the hypothesis that TAAR1 partial
agonism promotes wakefulness by modulating serotonergic arousal systems. We will determine whether
TAAR1 partial agonists modulate the activity of DRN serotonergic neurons using in vivo Ca2+ microendoscopy
in Fev-Cre mice and assess whether blockade of serotonergic signaling attenuates the wake-promoting effects
of TAAR1 partial agonists. We have found that TAAR1 deletion elevates high-frequency gamma EEG activity,
suggesting that TAAR1 modulates cortical function. To determine whether TAAR1-mediated elevation of
gamma activity is conserved across species and specific to TAAR1, we will investigate basal sleep/wake
physiology and conduct quantitative EEG analyses in Taar1 KO and OE rats and Taar2-9 KO mice. Together,
these Aims will begin to establish the neural circuitry and mechanisms that underlie the efficacy of TAAR1
agonists.

results.title: Trace Amine Receptors in Non Human Primates
results.abstract: DESCRIPTION (provided by applicant): Trace amines, distinguishable from the well-characterized biogenic amines, have been known to exist in mammalian brain for over 25 years. The recent discovery of a family of mammalian trace amine receptors (TARs) presents a significant new resource for exploring the physiological and pharmacological relevance of trace amines in brain (Borowsky et al, 2001). In conjunction with this finding is the unanticipated discovery that drugs of abuse, ranging from amphetamine, MDMA, LSD, as well as dopamine stimulate rat TAR1-mediated cAMP formation at pharmacologically relevant concentrations (Bunzow et al, 2001). Accordingly, trace amine receptors may directly or indirectly contribute to psychostimulant and hallucinogenic drug effects. As human and rodent trace amine receptors diverge in structure, subtype number and brain distribution, we postulate that non-human primates will provide a more suitable model for uncovering the physiological and pharmacological relevance of trace amine subtypes. In this regard, pilot studies indicate a 96% sequence identity for TAR1 in non-human primate and human. To establish fundamental information needed to explore TAR subtype function, we will investigate non-human primate TAR subtype structure, pharmacology, signal transduction and brain distribution. Aim 1 will determine whether human TAR subtypes (TAR1, 3, 4, 5) and structurally related orphan receptors (GPR57, GPR58 and PNR) exist in nonhuman primates. Based on these results, Aim 2 will utilize luciferase assays sensitive to different signal transduction pathways to uncover agonists as well as antagonists that block agonist-induced receptor activation. To characterize the pharmacological profile of these receptors, radioreceptor assays will be developed from lead compound(s) identified from luciferase assays. Aim 3 will map TAR subtype mRNA and protein distribution in primate brain using in situ hybridization, real-time RT-PCR and immunohistochemistry, to discern which receptor subtypes are expressed in brain for further exploration. Our pilot studies suggest that primate TARs are direct targets of psychostimulant drugs of abuse in brain. The proposed studies will form the basis for investigating the physiological and pharmacological relevance of trace amine receptors in a primate model, and may provide novel leads for developing therapeutic agents to treat addiction and possibly neuropsychiatric disorders.

results.title: Mechanisms of Prion Misfolding
results.abstract:
ABSTRACT- area 07
Prion diseases are a group of aggressive, lethal and incurable neurodegenerative disorders. The hallmark
pathological event in these maladies is the misfolding, aggregation and brain deposition of ¿scrapie¿ Prion
protein (PrPSc), which leads to spongiform degeneration of brain neurons. Unfortunately, a major gap exists in
our understanding of how the conformational conversion of PrP ultimately kills neurons. Recent in vitro studies
suggest that molecular chaperones may be key factors mediating PrP conversion and neuronal dysfunction.
However, the functional relevance of this finding is unknown. My central hypothesis is that targeted
expression of molecular chaperones can suppress PrP misfolding and PrP-mediated neurodegeneration. To
that end, I created a novel and powerful Drosophila model of sporadic prion disease in which wild type PrP
from Hamster converts into PrPSc¿like conformations and causes spongiform degeneration. Supporting my
hypothesis, human Hsp70 prevents PrP misfolding and protects against PrP-dependent neurotoxicity in
transgenic flies. The overall goal of this project is to define the role of molecular chaperones in PrP misfolding
by a multidisciplinary approach that combines the power of Drosophila genetics with mammalian cellular
systems and mice. My specific aims are: 1) Genetic, biochemical and pharmacological approaches to study
Hsp70 protection against PrP misfolding and neurotoxicity in Drosophila; 2) Determination of the ability of the
Unfolded Protein Response components XBP1s and Grp58 to suppress PrP misfolding and neurotoxicity in
Drosophila; 3) Role of molecular chaperones in prion replication in simplified mammalian systems, and 4)
Potential therapeutic role of Hsp70 in mouse models of prion diseases. I anticipate that our studies will
contribute to better understand the molecular basis underlying PrP conversion. In addition, by exploring the
role of chaperone-inducing compounds in flies and mice, I may discover effective and innovative therapeutic
interventions for treating these devastating and yet incurable diseases. 1. SPECIFIC AIMS
Prion diseases, or Transmissible Spongiform Encephalopathies (TSE), are lethal neurodegenerative disorders
with sporadic, genetic, and infectious origins. The hallmark pathological event in these maladies is the
conformational change (¿conversion¿) and brain deposition of ¿scrapie¿ Prion Protein (PrPSc). Unfortunately, a
major gap exists in our understanding of the mechanisms triggering PrP misfolding in these incurable
disorders. A major focus in prion biology is transmissibility, a unique feature of prion disorders. However, the
most common TSE in humans, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD), has a sporadic origin. Thus, we have
concentrated our effort on dissecting the mechanisms of sporadic TSE in an invertebrate model of prion
conversion. We have observed that transgenic flies expressing wild type PrP from Hamster display spongiform
degeneration associated to PrPSc-like conformation. Our preliminary studies also suggest that molecular
chaperones may be key factors mediating PrP misfolding. Therefore, our central HYPOTHESIS is that targeted
expression of molecular chaperones can suppress PrP misfolding and PrP-mediated neurodegeneration. The
overall goal of this project is to precisely define the role of molecular chaperones in PrP misfolding and
neurotoxicity by combining the power of Drosophila genetics with mammalian cellular systems and mouse
models of the disease. We will determine how the heat shock chaperone Hsp70, the endoplasmic reticulum
(ER)-chaperone Grp58, the Unfolded Protein Response (UPR) transcription factor XBP1s, and a battery of
chaperone-inducing compounds modify PrP misfolding and neurotoxicity in transgenic flies, scrapie-infected
mammalian cells, and in scrapie-infected mice. I propose the following specific aims:
¿ Specific Aim 1: Genetic, biochemical and pharmacological approaches to study Hsp70 protection
 against PrP misfolding and neurotoxicity in Drosophila
Rationale and planned studies: The levels of Hsp70 increase several fold in scrapie-infected mice and in CJD
patients (1, 2). We show here that targeted expression of human Hsp70 prevents PrP misfolding and alleviates
PrP-induced degeneration in Drosophila brain neurons. Thus, our working hypothesis is that Hsp70 modulates
PrP misfolding and that genetic and pharmacological induction of chaperones may serve as therapeutic tools
against prion diseases. To test this hypothesis, we will use the flexibility of the Drosophila system to study the
role of Hsp70 and its co-chaperones Hsp40 and CHIP to regulate PrP misfolding, cellular distribution and
neurotoxicity. We will also identify chaperone-inducing compounds with the ability to prevent PrP misfolding.
¿ Specific Aim 2: Determination of the ability of UPR components to suppress PrP misfolding and
 neurotoxicity in Drosophila
Rationale and planned studies: XBP1s is a potent transcription factor that binds and activates the promoters of
several chaperones, including Hsp70 and the ER chaperone Grp58. XBP1s overexpression in cultured cells
protects against PrP misfolding associated to ER stress, while Grp58 is upregulated in scrapie-infected mice
as well as in brains of patients with sporadic CJD (3-5). Thus, we hypothesize that targeted expression of
Grp58 and/or XBP1s may suppress PrP-induced neurodegeneration in vivo. To prove this, we will overexpress
mammalian Grp58 or XBP1s together with PrP in transgenic flies to determine the dynamics of PrP misfolding
and neurotoxicity in vivo.
¿ Specific Aim 3: Role of molecular chaperones in prion replication in simplified mammalian systems
Rationale and planned studies: Our preliminary data and published reports suggest that molecular chaperones
and UPR components recognize and target misfolded PrP for Proteasome degradation (4). Thus, we
hypothesize that Hsp70, Grp58 or XBP1s may be capable of modulating PrPSc conversion. We will measure
the conversion rate of PrPSc in an in vitro replication system (6) and in chronically infected rodent
neuroblastoma cells in conditions of increased or decreased Hsp70, Grp58 or XBP1s activity.
¿ Specific Aim 4: Potential therapeutic role of Hsp70 in mouse models of TSE
Rationale and planned studies: Our working hypothesis predicts that stimulating Hsp70 expression should
block or delay the onset of prion diseases in rodents. To test this, we will use genetic and pharmacological
approaches to modulate Hsp70 in scrapie-infected mice and then evaluate the onset of TSE. Transgenic mice
overexpressing Hsp70 (7) or lacking the inducible Hsp70 genes (8) will be infected with PrPSc and,
subsequently, PrPSc conversion and neurotoxicity will be measured. Also, normal mice infected with PrPSc will
be treated with chaperone-inducing compounds and their beneficial effects will be measured.
2. BACKGROUND AND SIGNIFICANCE
2.1. PrP and Prion disorders. Prion disorders or TSE comprise an incurable class of neurological disorders
that affect humans and other mammals, and lead to rapid spongiform degeneration of the brain and,
eventually, death (9, 10). In humans, conformational change and deposition of the Prion Protein (PrP) cause
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD), Fatal Familial Insomnia, Gerstmann-Str¿usssler-Scheinker syndrome, and
other disorders with infectious origins: Kuru, variant CJD and iatrogenic CJD, suggesting that common
mechanisms might mediate PrP conversion in all TSE. Without available palliative treatments, patients
suffering from TSE usually die within one year of the first clinical symptoms. PrP is a membrane-anchored
glycoprotein highly enriched in the brain (9, 10). The physiological role of PrP is under debate, although it is not
necessary for cell survival (9). PrP undergoes an irreversible conformational change from the cellular, soluble
?¿helix-rich isoform (PrPC) to a pathological, insoluble ?¿sheet-rich isoform known as PrPSc. PrPSc can be
distinguished from PrPC by its partial protease resistance, its insolubility in non-ionic detergents, and is
specifically recognized by conformational antibodies (9-11). According to the protein-only hypothesis (10),
PrPSc propagates its abnormal conformation using PrPC as substrate. But the exact molecular processes
involved in PrP conversion and neurotoxicity are still unknown. Hence, concerted and sustained research in
different model systems will contribute to a better understanding of PrP biogenesis and pathogenesis.
2.2. Sporadic Prion diseases. Prion diseases are unique within the group of debilitating brain disorders in that
they exist as sporadic, inherited or infectious forms. Sporadic prion diseases account for 85% of all Prion
disorders in humans. In patients with sporadic CJD and FFI, wild type PrP spontaneously converts into PrPSc in
the brain to induce pathogenesis by mechanisms largely unknown. Age is a well-established risk factor
associated with sporadic prion disorders, suggesting that deterioration of the physiological mechanisms that
control cellular homeostasis is critical for PrP conversion. Additionally, a polymorphism in the regulatory region
of the PrP gene increases the risk for Prion diseases, suggesting that genetic variability affecting PrP
expression levels might contribute to sporadic disease (12). Moreover, transgenic mice overexpressing wild
type PrP display neuronal loss, astroglyosis, primary myopathy and PrP deposition (13, 14). All these
observations suggest that the expression level of wild type PrP could be critical for the spontaneous
conversion of PrP and for the development of Prion-related neuropathology. Therefore, model systems in
which the amounts of PrP could be deliberately modulated and monitored will be instrumental to understand
sporadic PrP misfolding and its role in pathogenesis.
2.3. Prion disorders, ER stress, the Unfolded Protein Response and molecular chaperones. Perturbation
of Proteasome or ER function may result in accumulation of misfolded proteins in the ER lumen, a condition
termed ¿ER stress¿. To avert ER stress cells activate an integrated intracellular signaling cascade: the
Unfolded Protein Response (UPR). During UPR, activated ATF6 and IRE1? coordinately cleave the X-box-
binding protein (Xbp1) mRNA to produce XBP1s, a new transcription factor. XBP1s directly activates ER stress
genes to facilitate the refolding and degradation of misfolded proteins. Indirect evidence links prion
pathogenesis to ER alteration and chaperone induction: the chaperones Hsp70, Grp78/Bip, Grp94 and Grp58
are upregulated in the brain of CJD patients and in murine scrapie models (2, 4). Moreover, the effect of
molecular chaperones on the neurotoxicity of misfolded proteins has been investigated in a diverse range of
disease models. For instance, Bonini's group found that Hsp70 overexpression suppressed the loss of
dopaminergic neurons induced by ?-synuclein in a fly model of Parkinson's disease, while its co-chaperone
Hsp40 showed protective effects in a fly model of spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 (SCA1) (15, 16). Interestingly,
mouse models of SCA1 and spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy confirmed that Hsp70 mitigates
neurodegeneration (17). Moreover, my collaborator C. Soto recently found that overexpression of Grp58 and
XBP1s in N2a cells prevent PrPSc accumulation and protects against PrPSc neurotoxicity (4, 5). Despite all
these data, the protective activity of XBP1s, Hsp70 or Gpr58 against prion pathogenesis has not been
determined in vivo. We propose here that our PrP transgenic flies are well suited to assess the ability of
components of the UPR pathway to prevent PrP misfolding and neurotoxicity in vivo.
2.4. How can PrP transgenic flies contribute to understand prion biology? The fruit fly Drosophila
melanogaster has been a favored tool for genetic studies for over 100 years and is an excellent model system
to study development, signal transduction, cell biology and immunity. The relevance of Drosophila to humans
is perhaps best illustrated by the realization that more than 60% of the genes identified in human diseases
have counterparts in Drosophila. Research using Drosophila is quite relevant for understanding human
neurobiology because flies and humans share highly conserved cellular organization and function of the
nervous system. In fact, a number of human neurological disorders caused by gain-of-function mechanisms
have been studied in flies, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, tauopathies, polyglutamine
disorders, and non-coding expansions (18). In addition, these fly models have confirmed the potential of
Drosophila in the identification of genetic and pharmacological suppressors of neurodegeneration (15, 16, 18).
We believe that PrP-expressing flies can be a key tool to better understand the molecular mechanisms
involved in PrP misfolding and/or neurotoxicity. However, the development of Drosophila models of prion
disorders has been challenging because two independent groups failed to induce prion-dependent
neurotoxicity in flies (19, 20). More recently, one of these groups reported that expression of the mutant
PrPP101L, but not wild type mouse PrP, induce degeneration in the fly brain (21). Thus, new approaches have
been considered here to generate a definitive fly model of sporadic Prion conversion and neurotoxicity.
2.5. Relevance and potential benefits for human health. Considerable effort has been devoted to isolating
the infectious agent in prion disorders, identifying the mechanism of infectivity, and establishing the conversion
mechanisms. However, we still have a very limited understanding of the molecular and cellular mechanisms
involved in PrP misfolding and neurotoxicity. A key challenge, therefore, is to identify the proteins and
pathways mediating PrP misfolding. Thus, it is of paramount importance to study prion diseases in a
combination of models of prion pathobiology, including transgenic Drosophila, mammalian neuronal cell
cultures and mice. Our transgenic fly model provides a powerful tool to investigate the mechanisms of PrP
conversion and prion-dependent neurotoxicity. The validation of the novel cellular pathways identified in flies
into established mammalian models will demonstrate their physiological relevance, and may provide new
mechanistic insights into PrP misfolding and pathobiology. In addition, by exploring the role of chaperone-
inducing compounds in flies and mice, our research could have translational consequences by discovering
effective and innovative therapeutic interventions for treating these devastating and yet incurable diseases.
3. PRELIMINARY RESULTS
This proposal takes advantage of the expertise of my collaborators and my own in Drosophila genetics and
neurobiology (myself), molecular genetics, transgenic mice and Drosophila biology (Diego Rincon-Limas,
UTMB), in vitro and in vivo Prion biology (Claudio Soto, UTMB), Prion biology and ER stress (Claudio Hetz,
Harvard Medical School), and biochemistry of chaperones (Jose Barral, UTMB). I place a high value in
assembling a strong team of collaborators, which will also be key to the success of my project.
We present here a brief summary of our preliminary results demonstrating PrP conversion and neurotoxicity in
Drosophila, and provide recent experimental evidence for the direct role of molecular chaperones in mediating
PrP misfolding and neurotoxicity in transgenic flies: 1) Mammalian PrP induces spongiform degeneration in
flies; 2) Mammalian PrP undergoes PrPSc-like conformation in transgenic flies as indicated by insolubility in
non-ionic detergents, fibrillogenesis and immunodetection by PrPSc conformational antibodies, and 3) Human
Hsp70 prevents PrP misfolding and protects Drosophila brain neurons against PrP neurotoxicity. Thus, we
demonstrate that our innovative approaches are suitable and appropriate towards creating an invertebrate
model of sporadic PrP conversion and to identify in vivo suppressors of PrP neurotoxicity. Moreover, our
observations validate the potential for success of the proposed research.
3.1. Hamster PrP induces spongiform degeneration in Drosophila. We selected PrP from Syrian Golden
Hamster for modelling prion disorders in flies to ensure the safety of prion handling in the lab due to a well-
documented species barrier between rodents and humans. Transgenic flies carrying wild type PrP will allow us
to model, study and understand aspects of PrP pathobiology associated to sporadic prion diseases, the most
prevalent form of prion pathologies in humans. For this, the open reading frame of wild type PrP from hamster
was cloned into the Drosophila pUAST vector to generate transgenic flies. Our PrP transgenic flies will help us
understand the conformational changes of PrP and its neurotoxic consequences in a genetic tractable model.
Vacuolation is a disease hallmark of the Transmissible Spongiform Encephalopathies. In scrapie-infected
hamsters neuronal vacuolation is very obvious due to the large size of these cells (Fig 1A, arrow). Flies
expressing PrP and aged for 30 days also show prominent degeneration, revealing abundant holes in the
neuropile (Fig. 1B, arrows). Since the cell body of the Drosophila brain neuron is very small and contains little
cytoplasm (Fig. 1B, arrowheads), vacuolation is difficult to document in conventional histological preparations.
By ultrastructural analysis of cell morphology we clearly determined that Drosophila brain neurons undergo
vacuolar (¿spongiform¿) degeneration (Fig. 1C, arrows). Therefore, EXPRESSION AND ACCUMULATION OF WILD
TYPE PRP LEAD TO SPONGIFORM DEGENERATION OF DROSOPHILA BRAIN NEURONS, A HALLMARK OF PRION
NEUROPATHOLOGY. For a more detailed study of PrP neurotoxicity, we expressed PrP in the mushroom bodies,
which are composed of the projections of 5,000 neurons (the Kenyon cells) that form five thick lobes: Two ?,
two ? and one ?. 40 day-old control flies expressing LacZ in the mushroom bodies showed strong ?, ? and ?
lobes with normal morphology (Fig. 1D). As expected, PrP induced progressive degeneration of the mushroom
bodies, although the ? and ? lobes seemed the most sensitive to PrP neurotoxicity, while the ? lobes seemed
more resilient (Fig. 1E). We, then, determined if the degeneration of the axonal projections induced by PrP was
associated to a reduction in the number of Kenyon cells. The surface occupied by the Kenyon cells was
dramatically reduced in older flies compared with controls, indicating a correlation between axonal
degeneration and cell loss (Figs. 1F and G).

 infected hamster and transgenic flies expressing

 when compared to controls.
3.2. Mammalian PrP aggregates in amyloid fibers in Drosophila. To investigate the presence of fibrils by
transmission electron microscopy (TEM), we separated the insoluble fraction from head extracts of 40 day-old
flies expressing either PrP or LacZ (control). The PrP flies contained abundant electron-dense materials with
fibrillar organization (Fig. 2A). This fibrillar material was comparable in size and shape to the fibrils obtained
from scrapie-infected hamsters using the methodology reported by S. Prusiner (22). However, the LacZ flies
contained very little electron-dense material consistent with cellular debris (Fig. 2B). Therefore, accumulation
of fibrillar aggregates in old flies expressing PrP is consistent with PrP misfolding, which could be the
neurotoxic conformation in flies.
Figure 2. PrP forms amyloid fibers in transgenic flies. The insoluble fraction of 40
day-old flies expressing PrP (A) or LacZ (B) was collected and observed by TEM at
47,000X. The control flies expressing LacZ accumulate amorphous electron-dense
material. In flies expressing PrP the electron-dense material are more abundant and
contain fibrillar structures consistent with amyloid fibers.
3.3. Mammalian PrP acquires a PrPSc-like conformation in Drosophila. To determine if the neurotoxic
effects induced by PrP in flies are associated to the acquisition of an abnormal, pathologic PrP conformation,
we compared the biochemical properties of hamster PrPSc and PrP expressed in transgenic flies. We
characterized the structure of PrP by using a conformational antibody that discriminates normal (PrPC) and
disease-specific (PrPSc) conformations (11). As shown in figure 3, PrPSc, but not PrPC from hamster, is
immunoprecipitated by 15B3. Then, we performed immunoprecipitation with 15B3 in transgenic flies
expressing LacZ or hamster PrP. 15B3 detected abnormal PrP from young and old flies, although the level of
precipitated PrP increased in older flies, suggesting that the 15B3 epitope accumulates over time. This result
 indicates that PrP spontaneously and progressively assumes a PrPSc-like
conformation in transgenic flies, thus, supporting the adequacy of our model to
study sporadic TSE.
Figure 3. 15B3 identifies a PrPSc-like conformation in flies. Immunoprecipitation of PrPSc-like epitopes from
brain extracts from healthy (PrPC) and scrapie-infected (PrPSc) hamsters or transgenic flies expressing LacZ (Tg-
LacZ) and hamster PrP (Tg-PrP) using the 15B3 antibody. PrP was detected in Western blot using the 3F4 anti-
PrP antibody. 15B3 specifically precipitates PrPSc (arrowhead), but not PrPC. 15B3 also detected PrP from flies
(arrowheads), while the lane containing LacZ-expressing flies rendered no signal. 40 day-old flies produced a
bigger reactivity than 1 day-old flies.
Disease-associated PrPSc is insoluble and resistant to denaturing agents, including heat, urea and Guanidine
thiocyanate; however, high concentration of chemical denaturants renders PrPSc soluble. We compared the
biochemical properties of PrPSc from hamsters and PrP from transgenic flies by subjecting extracts to
Guanidine and, then, determining PrP solubility in non-ionic detergents. Both PrPSc from hamster and PrP from
transgenic flies are solubilized at 2M concentration of Guanidine (fig. 4). The comparable Guanidine sensitivity
 shown here suggests that the conformation of PrP in transgenic
 flies is similar to that of PrPSc from hamsters.
 Figure 4. The PrPSc-like conformation in flies is sensitive to denaturing agents. Extracts
 from scrapie-infected hamster (left) and PrP transgenic flies (Tg-PrP) were treated with a .5
 to 2 M gradient of guanidine thiocyanate. Then, the samples were incubated in 10% sarkosyl
 and the insoluble fraction was subjected to western blot using the 3F4 antibody. Treatments
 of 2 M Guanidine (circled) rendered PrPSc from hamsters and PrPSc-like from flies soluble.
Another typical feature of disease-associated PrP (PrPSc) is its partial resistance to Proteinase K (PK). We
subjected brain extracts from PrP transgenic flies to mild PK digestions and found increased PK-resistance in
40 day-old flies compared to the 1 day-old flies (Fig. 5). This result supports the progressive conformational
changes of PrP described in figure 3. However, PrP from transgenic flies does not exhibit the shift in molecular
weight characteristic of infectious PrPSc after PK digestion (10). Therefore, flies do not produce a PrP
conformer consistent with the prototypical, infectious PrPSc. Even if the PrPSc-like conformer generated by
transgenic flies is not infectious, the conformational changes documented in older flies are consistent with
intermediate PrP conformations (denoted PrP* or PrPL) that might be relevant in disease progression (23).

increases in older flies.
 3.4. Human Hsp70 protects against PrP neurotoxicity and prevents PrP misfolding in flies. Prion
disorders and other protein deposition neuropathologies involve protein misfolding and aggregation. Molecular
chaperones recognize these misfolded proteins and contribute to their refolding and degradation. To directly
assess the ability of Hsp70 to protect against PrP-dependent neurotoxicity, we combined constructs
expressing human Hsp70 [shown to rescue neurotoxicity in flies (16)] and PrP in the fly mushroom bodies.
Control flies expressing two neutral transgenes (GFP and LacZ) show perfectly organized mushroom body
lobes after 45 days (Fig. 6A, arrow). On the other hand, 45 day-old flies expressing PrP and GFP display
prominent degeneration of mushroom body lobes (Fig. 6B). Remarkably, substituting the reporter GFP for the
molecular chaperone Hsp70 clearly protects mushroom body morphology (Fig. 6C and D). This protective
activity of Hsp70 is exerted directly on PrP since Hsp70 does not modify the levels of PrP transcripts as
 measured by quantitative RT-PCR (not shown). Next,
 we determined whether Hsp70 neuroprotection was
 mediated by direct effects on PrP conformation. We
 found that flies co-expressing Hsp70 and PrP do not
 accumulate insoluble PrP (Fig. 6E). Moreover, the
 15B3-reactive conformations almost disappear in flies
 co-expressing Hsp70 and PrP (Fig. 6F). Finally, we
 found that Hsp70 co-localizes with PrP in axonal
 aggregates (Fig. 6G-I). Overall, these results indicate
 that Hsp70 directly interacts with PrP, prevents PrP
conversion, and protects against PrP-dependent
neurotoxicity in transgenic flies.

4. RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS
? Specific Aim 1: Genetic, biochemical and pharmacological approaches to study Hsp70 protection
 against PrP misfolding and neurotoxicity in Drosophila
Rationale and hypothesis: The levels of Hsp70 increase several fold in mice infected with scrapie as well as in
CJD patients (1, 2). However, the functional relevance of this finding is unknown. Interestingly, our preliminary
data indicate that targeted expression of human Hsp70 modulates PrP misfolding and alleviates PrP-induced
neurodegeneration in Drosophila brain neurons (Fig. 6). We hypothesize that genetic and pharmacological
modulation of Hsp70 activity may prevent PrP misfolding and protect against PrP-mediated
neurodegeneration. Thus, we will first examine the consequence of co-expressing Hsp70 and PrP in
transgenic flies. Then we will determine the ability of chaperone-inducing drugs to prevent PrP misfolding and
PrP-induced neurodegeneration.
 a. Biochemical, cellular and histological characterization of flies expressing PrP coupled with normal
 Hsp70, overexpressed Hsp70 or dominant-negative Hsp70: insolubility, conformational antibodies,
 subcellular distribution and ultrastructural studies.
 b. Determine the role of other heat shock chaperones or co-chaperones, such as Hsp40 or CHIP (17), in
 enhancing Hsp70 function by co-expression experiments in PrP-expressing flies.
 c. Assess the ability of the chaperone-inducing compounds Geldanamycyn, 17-allylamino-17-demethoxy-
 geldanamycin (17AAG), Geranylgeranylacetone (GGA), and Arimoclomol (17) to suppress PrP
 misfolding and neurotoxicity in flies.
Expected results and potential problems: The procedures for this aim have been shown in the Preliminary
Results. We expect that human Hsp70 will decrease PrP misfolding and neurotoxicity in Drosophila. In
contrast, we anticipate that co-expression of PrP with a dominant negative form of Hsp70 (HSC4K71S) will
increase PrP misfolding and accelerate neurodegenerative phenotypes. We also expect that at least one of the
chaperone-inducing drugs will suppress PrP misfolding. However, if none of the drugs produce clear results we
will feed flies with combinations of two drugs to try to potentiate their effects. We may also encounter that some
PrP phenotypes could be too strong to suppress by Hsp70. In this case, we could co-express Hsp70 and
Hsp40 or increase the levels of Hsp70 expression by generating a Drosophila strain carrying two or more
copies of the Hsp70 transgene.
Significance of results: Under cellular stress conditions Hsp70 is thought to prevent aggregation and/or assist
in the refolding of misfolded proteins. However, the in vivo role of Hsp70 in the pathogenesis of prion diseases
is largely unknown. Thus, the proposed work provides the opportunity to comprehensively address the ability of
Hsp70 to modulate PrP-mediated neurodegeneration in a transgenic animal. If we can prove that directed
expression of Hsp70 or pharmacological induction of Hsp70 suppresses PrP-dependent neurotoxicity, our
results will have profound implications for future design of therapeutic strategies against prion pathology.
? Specific Aim 2: Determination of the ability of UPR components to suppress PrP misfolding and
 neurotoxicity in Drosophila
Rationale and hypothesis: The ER chaperone Grp58 is upregulated in scrapie-infected mice as well as in
brains of patients with CJD (3). Indeed, XBP1s and Grp58 overexpression protects against PrPSc toxicity in
cultured cells, while their ablation by siRNA enhances it (4, 5). However, no evidence is yet available on the
functional interaction of PrP with XBP1s and Grp58 in vivo. Inspired by these studies, we decided to test the
effect of Grp58 and XBP1s in our PrP-expressing flies. We hypothesize that targeted expression of Grp58
and XBP1s may prevent PrP misfolding and suppress PrP-induced neurodegeneration in Drosophila
brain neurons. To verify this, our newly generated transgenic flies expressing mouse Grp58 and XBP1s will
be combined with the PrP transgene to assess the course of PrP misfolding.
 a. Biochemical, cellular, histological and behavioral characterization of flies expressing PrP coupled with
 overexpressed Grp58, overexpressed XBP1s or dominant-negative XBP1. PrP insolubility, cellular
 distribution and neurodegeneration will be compared among these groups.
 b. Genetic experiments will be conducted to test the potential synergism of Grp58 and XBP1 with the
 Hsp70 transgenes used in Aim1.
Expected results and potential problems: Murine XBP1s and Grp58 should suppress PrP misfolding and PrP-
induced neurodegeneration in Drosophila. In contrast, co-expression with XBP1dn, which binds target DNA
sequences but cannot activate chaperone transcription, should enhance PrP misfolding and neurotoxicity. In
addition, we should be able to determine whether Grp58 and XBP1s can alter PrP subcellular distribution.
What if single Grp58 and XBP1 transgenes have little effects on PrP flies? If this occurs, we will introduce
additional copies of these transgenes to boost their expression. Alternatively, we will co-express Grp58 with
Hsp70 and XBP1 to see whether their combinations are more effective than expression of either one alone.
Significance of results: Proper understanding of the molecular cross-talk between different chaperones that
control protein misfolding, trafficking and clearance is crucial to determine which cellular processes mediate
neuronal dysfunction. The experiments described here will answer whether expression of Grp58 and/or XBP1s
are sufficient to suppress or delay PrP-induced neurodegeneration in vivo. Our results will be valuable to
delineate the extent to which Grp58 and XBP1s participate in prion diseases and may provide new information
into the mechanisms of neuronal death. Since the development of several chaperone modulators has already
reached clinical phases, our results will be relevant for the design of novel therapies for prion disorders.
? Specific Aim 3: Role of molecular chaperones in prion replication in simplified mammalian systems
Rationale and hypothesis: To continue building on our preliminary data that molecular chaperones prevent PrP
misfolding in flies, we will investigate the functional relevance of Hsp70, Grp58 and XBP1s in PrP conversion in
vitro and in scrapie-infected neuroblastoma cells. In addition, overwhelming evidence indicates that chaperone-
inducing compounds are crucial modulators of protein aggregation and neurodegeneration (17). Thus, we
hypothesize that by modifying the activity of molecular chaperones we can modulate PrPC to PrPSc
conversion in vitro and in cell culture. These experiments are critical to determine the relevance of Hsp70,
Grp58 and XBP1s in modulating PrP misfolding in mammalian systems.
 a. Evaluate the effect of adding or depleting Hsp70 and Grp58 on PrP replication in vitro using the potent
 Protein Misfolding Cyclic Amplification (PMCA) technology (6).
 b. Study the influence of Hsp70, ER chaperones and XBP1 on prion conversion in chronically infected
 neuroblastoma cells transfected with overexpression or siRNA constructs.
 c. Determine whether the chaperone-inducing compounds described in Specific Aim 1 can modify prion
 replication in cellular models.
Expected results and potential problems: These studies will allow us to better understand the involvement of
Hsp70, Grp58 and XBP1s in prion conversion and replication in simplified mammalian systems. If our
hypothesis is correct, PMCA experiments should reveal a decrease of PrP conversion or even a complete
inhibition of this process in vitro in the presence of exogenous Hsp70 and Grp58. Conversely, we should see
an acceleration of PrPSc formation in the absence of these two proteins. We also expect to determine whether
Hsp70, XBP1s, or pharmacological chaperones alter prion replication in chronically infected cells. One of the
potential problems could be that the repeated sonication cycles may alter protein complexes. To rule out this
possibility, we will perform amplification experiments without sonication (equivalent to 1 PMCA cycle), which
enables a 4-8 fold PrPSc amplification (6). If the siRNA constructs are insufficient to knock out Hsp70 or XBP1
proteins, or if there is any potential functional redundancy, we will consider using dominant negative constructs
carrying a dead ATPase domain. On the other hand, if we do not see any effect on PrPSc replication when
Hsp70 is overexpressed, we will consider co-expressing it with Hsp40.
Significance of results: Hetz et al. suggested recently that PrPSc replication induces ER-stress (4). It is
possible, therefore, that ER chaperones are up-regulated in an attempt to correct misfolded PrPSc or to remove
it via the delivery of the proteins towards the proteosomal degradation pathway. Thus, these studies will
determine whether XBP1, Grp58, Hsp70 or the general repertoire of inducible heat shock chaperones have an
influence on PrPSc replication and will reveal potential strategies for preventing PrPSc formation. More
importantly, we will assess the ability of chaperone-inducing compounds to slow down PrP misfolding and
accumulation in a mammalian cellular system. These results will be critical to determine which compound(s) is
the most effective and, therefore, which one should be used in mice.
? Specific Aim 4: Potential therapeutic role of Hsp70 in mouse models of TSE
Rationale and hypothesis: Compelling experimental evidence indicates that genetic and pharmacological
modulation of Hsp70 has tremendous potential in neurodegenerative diseases (17). However, the in vivo role
of Hsp70 in mammalian models of prion disease is completely unknown. Based on our preliminary results, we
hypothesize that Hsp70 can modify PrP conversion and neuropathology in scrapie-infected mice. To
prove this, we will first investigate the onset of TSE in transgenic mice overexpressing Hsp70 (7) or lacking
inducible Hsp70 (8). Also, scrapie-infected mice will be treated with the most effective chaperone-inducing
compound, as determined in PrP-expressing flies and mammalian neuronal cultures.
 a. Hsp70 transgenic [W. Dillmann, (7)] and knockout [Mutant Mouse Regional Resource Centers
 (MMRRC) (8)] mice, as well as appropriate control animals, will be inoculated intracerebrally with
 Rocky Mountain Laboratory (RML) prions. We will evaluate disease progression, Hsp70 expression
 levels, PrPSc accumulation and the extent of neuronal death.
 b. We will also test the ability of the most effective chaperone-inducing compound(s) identified in Aims 1
 and 3 to alter TSE pathogenesis in rodents. These compounds have been used in murine models and
 their administration and dosage are well documented. They will be administered to wild type mice
 before or after inoculation with RML prions. These animals will be evaluated as outlined above.
Expected results and potential problems: The PI has assembled a team with ample experience in the
generation, breeding and genotyping of transgenic mice, prion inoculation procedures and in the pathological
and biochemical analysis of the mouse brain. Thus, we do not anticipate any technical problem in this regard. If
our hypothesis is correct, mice overexpressing Hsp70 will experience a delay in the onset of clinical disease
and in prion replication. Conversely, in Hsp70 null mice we expect that both prion replication and onset of
clinical disease will be substantially accelerated. We also expect that the best chaperone-inducing compound
identified in flies and mammalian cells will work effectively in scrapie-infected mice. However, the effects might
not be clear due to the long incubation time of the disease. In this case, we will try to accelerate the onset of
TSE by using the Tg20 mice, which have substantially shorter incubation period than wild type mice (24). In
addition, if several drugs are effective against PrP misfolding and neurotoxicity in flies and N2A cells, we will try
to test the best combinatorial regimes in mice. If Hsp70 overexpression alone does not delay TSE onset, we
will investigate if chaperone-inducing drugs can potentiate the effect of the Hsp70 transgene.
Significance of results: The demonstration that genetic and/or pharmacological induction of heat shock
chaperones blocks or delays neuropathology in scrapie-infected mice will have far-reaching consequences in
the prion field. This work is relatively simple and will provide important insights on the mechanisms leading to
PrP-inducing neurodegeneration in the mammalian brain. Importantly, it also has potential translational
applications by laying the foundation for developing a rational therapy for the incurable prion disorders.
DROSOPHILA METHODS-Transgenic flies and genetics: We will use transgenic flies expressing human Hsp70
[N. Bonini (16)], dominant negative Hsp70 (HSC4K71S, K. Palter), and mouse Grp58 and XBP1s (my
laboratory). UAS:LacZ (control), UAS:CD8-GFP (control) and OK107-Gal4 flies were obtained from the
Bloomington Drosophila Stock Center. Murine cDNAs encoding for unspliced (XBP1u) and dominant negative
(XBP1dn) XBP1 will be subcloned into pUAST and injected in Drosophila yw embryos by P-element
transformation. Crosses will be performed as follows: Females homozygous for the driver OK107 will be mated
with males bearing a PrP transgene combined with Hsp70, HSC4K71S, Grp58, XBP1s, XBP1dn, CD8-GFP or
bacterial LacZ transgenes. Cellular and Histo-pathological characterization: Fly brains will be dissected to
study the cellular distribution and/or aggregation of PrP. Double stains with antibodies for Hamster PrP (3F4,
Abcam) and for Drosophila Hsp70 (StressGen), mouse Grp58 (Stressgen), and mouse XBP1 (Santa Cruz
Biotech) will be conducted and analyzed by confocal microscopy. Whole-mount and paraffin-embedded brains
will be studied to assess mushroom body morphology. We will study cell death by TUNEL (Promega).
Ultrastructure of control aged flies and young PrP flies will be conducted in resin-embedded heads sectioned at
70 nm and observed by TEM. Pharmacological induction of chaperones in flies: Flies expressing PrP in
brain neurons will be raised in fly media containing 3, 12, 24 and 96 ¿g/ml Geldanamycin (BioMol, Inc). 17AAG
(Sigma) will be tested in parallel at similar concentrations. Also, we will use media containing 0.25%, 0.5% or
1% of the antiulcer drug GGA (Eisai Inc.) as described (25). Arimoclomol (Biorex) will be used at 10, 100 and
500 nM (26). Flies fed with media containing the vehicle alone (DMSO) will be used as control. To determine
the protective effect of the drugs, we will analyze PrP misfolding by separating the insoluble fraction and by
assessing chaperone induction in Western blots.
BIOCHEMISTRY- Preparation of tissue homogenates and Western blot: Fly heads will be homogenized and
immunoblotted onto nitrocellulose membranes after separation by 4-12% SDS/PAGE. The blots will be probed
with 3F4 and ?-tubulin (Sigma) antibodies and immunoreactivity will be visualized by enhanced
chemiluminescence (ECL, Amersham). Detergent solubility assay: Brain homogenates will be incubated in
the presence of 10% sarkosyl for 30 min at 4¿C, and treated with 5U benzonase and 0.3% sodium
phosphotungstate (NaPTA) as described (22). Then, supernatant, pellet and total fractions will be analyzed by
Western blots. Co-Immunoprecipitation: 50 heads from flies expressing Hsp70 and PrP will be homogenized
in RIPA buffer. Immunoprecipitation will be performed with the 3F4 antibody and protein A/G-Sepharose beads
(Amersham). The presence of PrP and Hsp70 will be evaluated by Western blot.
CELL CULTURE AND IN VITRO STUDIES-PMCA: This technique will be used to study PrP conversion dynamics in
vitro (6). Normal brain homogenate or cell lysate containing PrPC will be inoculated with PrPSc and loaded onto
a microsonicator Misonix programmed to perform cycles of 30 min incubation at 37¿C followed by a 40 s pulse
of sonication. Thus, exogenous recombinant human Hsp70 (StressGen) will be added to the brain substrate to
study the rate of PrPSc conversion. We will also study the rate of PMCA amplification using PrPC substrate
lacking Hsp70 by immunodepletion or by using a brain lysate from Hsp70 knock out mice. Newly generated
PrPSc will be measured by western blot after PK digestion to remove all PrPC. siRNA design: siRNA molecules
against mouse inducible Hsp70, XBP1s and a scrambled negative control will be purchased from Ambion.
siRNAs will be cloned into a pcDNA3-based vector with a U6 RNA promoter for expression. DNA constructs
and transfection: The pcDNA4 vector expressing murine XBP1s and Grp58 was provided by Dr. C. Hetz. The
human Hsp70 cDNA (N. Bonini) will be subcloned into pcDNA4. N2a cells will be stably transfected with
Hsp70, XBP1s or siRNA constructs using SuperFect (Qiagen). After 48h, cells will be selected with hygromicin
and individual clones will be obtained by limiting dilution. Cellular infection and drug treatment: Infectable
N2a neuroblastoma cells, mock or stably transfected with the constructs of interest, will be treated with mouse
RML scrapie. PrPSc propagation will be assessed by a dot blotting procedure in which lysis and protease
digestion are directly performed in the culture dish. Chaperone-inducing compounds will be added to the N2a
cells at the time of infection with RML prions. For Geldanamycin and 17GAA, we will use 18, 90, 180, and 360
nM in DMSO, which will be supplemented alone as control (27). For GGA we will use a concentration of 1 nM,
and 0.1 and 1 ¿M for Arimoclomol (25). PrPSc propagation will be assessed as outlined above.
LABORATORY ANIMALS-In vivo infectivity studies in mice: Hsp70-deficient mice (Hspa1a/Hspa1btm1Dix) (8) are
commercially available through the MMRRC (www.mmrc.org). Dr. Wolfgang Dillmann (UCSD) has agreed to
share his transgenic mice overexpressing rat inducible Hsp70 and their respective controls (CB6F1
background) (7). Groups of homozygous mice overexpressing Hsp70, Hsp70 null mice, as well as control
animals, will be inoculated with RML scrapie. Animals will be 4-5 weeks old at the time of inoculation.
Anesthetized animals will be injected stereotaxically in both right and left hippocampus with 1¿l of the PrPSc
inoculum. The onset of clinical disease will be measured by scoring the animals as described by C. Soto (6).
Terminally sick animals will be euthanized and the left-brain hemisphere will be frozen for biochemical studies
and the right-hemisphere will be prepared for histology. Immunohistochemical studies: The right hemisphere
of the brain will be fixed and embedded in paraplast. Serial sections (10¿m thick) will be stained with
hematoxylin-eosin or incubated with 6H4 anti-mouse PrP (Prionics). For co-localization, sections will be
sequentially incubated with anti-PrP antibody and rabbit anti-Hsp70 antibody followed by fluorescent
secondary antibodies, and then be analyzed by confocal microscopy. Neuronal counting will be assessed by
cresyl violet and by using the monoclonal anti-NeuN antibody (Chemicon). Pharmacological induction of
chaperones in scrapie-infected mice: Drug treatments will begin one week before infection and continue
until mice are 25 weeks old or until the first clinical symptoms appear. The best neuroprotective compound
identified in flies and N2A cells will be used. Potential treatment would be as follows: For 17AAG and
Arimoclomol, animals will receive 50 ¿l intraperitoneal injections of 25 and 10 mg/kg, respectively, three times
a week on alternate days (26, 28). For GGA, drug granules will be mixed with powdered rodent chow at a
concentration of 1% (25). Control animals treated only with vehicle will be used in all experiments. The onset of
clinical disease will be ¿blindly¿ measured by scoring the animals twice per week. Biochemical studies: To
detect PrPSc, a 10% brain homogenate will be first digested with 25 ¿g/mL PK at 37¿C for 1h. The equivalent of
30¿50 ¿g of total protein will be loaded onto 10% SDS-PAGE minigels and analysed by Western blotting. The
following primary antibodies will be used: 6H4 anti-mouse PrP; anti-iHsp70, anti-Hsp40 and anti-Hsp90
(Stressgen), and anti-tubulin. Immunoreactivity will be detected by ECL.
5. INVESTIGATOR QUALIFICATIONS. Although modeling human diseases in flies is not a highly innovative idea
anymore, I was a pioneer in this field. During my postdoc I was the first author of a Nature report that described
a fly model of Spinocerebellar ataxia type I, a polyglutamine disorder, and the isolation of genetic modifiers of
the neurotoxicity caused by the human expanded allele (15). I independently developed all the analytical tools
and approaches needed for characterizing our model since we started our project before other polyglutamine
models were published (18). This experience gave me the confidence to generate a fly model of prion
neuropathology despite the published reports describing the inadequacy of Drosophila as a model system for
prion pathogenesis (19, 20). This project is highly risky because it involves disproving the concept that
Drosophila is inadequate for studying prion pathogenesis. It also represents an intellectual challenge because I
had to learn a lot about prion biology, which is a field on its own due to transmissibility issues. As shown in the
preliminary results, I have considered novel approaches in the generation and characterization of my
Drosophila model of PrP conversion. I faced some of the difficulties described in previous reports while
generating my fly model. But exploring the flexible expression systems of Drosophila and combining cellular,
histological and biochemical tools of the Drosophila and prion fields produced the clear and impressive results
described here. Moreover, I bring a unique background to the field of prion biology that led me to challenge
PrP conformation with Hsp70, something that prion experts have not done yet. Additionally, I have assembled
a group of accomplished collaborators that will allow me to proceed with a multidisciplinary approach to
address key issues in my research project.
6. INNOVATIVE ASPECTS OF THIS PROPOSAL. I describe here the first genetic tractable model of sporadic PrP
conversion and neurotoxicity in transgenic Drosophila. Moreover, this is the first concerted effort to test
potential prion-modifying candidates in flies and mammalian systems. My creative thinking has identified the
first experimental evidence of the potential role of Hsp70 in PrP conversion. I will replicate this successful
approach with other candidates, including other molecular chaperones (alternative approaches are described
in the main project) Furthermore, I have already collected promising results with chaperone-inducing
compounds, although I am not ready to share these results (proprietary information). Although this project
presented daunting challenges from the start, the results presented here are the best demonstration of my
ability to face and solve complex problems.

results.title: Trace Amine Receptors in Non Human Primates
results.abstract: DESCRIPTION (provided by applicant): Trace amines, distinguishable from the well-characterized biogenic amines, have been known to exist in mammalian brain for over 25 years. The recent discovery of a family of mammalian trace amine receptors (TARs) presents a significant new resource for exploring the physiological and pharmacological relevance of trace amines in brain (Borowsky et al, 2001). In conjunction with this finding is the unanticipated discovery that drugs of abuse, ranging from amphetamine, MDMA, LSD, as well as dopamine stimulate rat TAR1-mediated cAMP formation at pharmacologically relevant concentrations (Bunzow et al, 2001). Accordingly, trace amine receptors may directly or indirectly contribute to psychostimulant and hallucinogenic drug effects. As human and rodent trace amine receptors diverge in structure, subtype number and brain distribution, we postulate that non-human primates will provide a more suitable model for uncovering the physiological and pharmacological relevance of trace amine subtypes. In this regard, pilot studies indicate a 96% sequence identity for TAR1 in non-human primate and human. To establish fundamental information needed to explore TAR subtype function, we will investigate non-human primate TAR subtype structure, pharmacology, signal transduction and brain distribution. Aim 1 will determine whether human TAR subtypes (TAR1, 3, 4, 5) and structurally related orphan receptors (GPR57, GPR58 and PNR) exist in nonhuman primates. Based on these results, Aim 2 will utilize luciferase assays sensitive to different signal transduction pathways to uncover agonists as well as antagonists that block agonist-induced receptor activation. To characterize the pharmacological profile of these receptors, radioreceptor assays will be developed from lead compound(s) identified from luciferase assays. Aim 3 will map TAR subtype mRNA and protein distribution in primate brain using in situ hybridization, real-time RT-PCR and immunohistochemistry, to discern which receptor subtypes are expressed in brain for further exploration. Our pilot studies suggest that primate TARs are direct targets of psychostimulant drugs of abuse in brain. The proposed studies will form the basis for investigating the physiological and pharmacological relevance of trace amine receptors in a primate model, and may provide novel leads for developing therapeutic agents to treat addiction and possibly neuropsychiatric disorders.

results.title: Trace Amine Receptors in Non Human Primates
results.abstract: DESCRIPTION (provided by applicant): Trace amines, distinguishable from the well-characterized biogenic amines, have been known to exist in mammalian brain for over 25 years. The recent discovery of a family of mammalian trace amine receptors (TARs) presents a significant new resource for exploring the physiological and pharmacological relevance of trace amines in brain (Borowsky et al, 2001). In conjunction with this finding is the unanticipated discovery that drugs of abuse, ranging from amphetamine, MDMA, LSD, as well as dopamine stimulate rat TAR1-mediated cAMP formation at pharmacologically relevant concentrations (Bunzow et al, 2001). Accordingly, trace amine receptors may directly or indirectly contribute to psychostimulant and hallucinogenic drug effects. As human and rodent trace amine receptors diverge in structure, subtype number and brain distribution, we postulate that non-human primates will provide a more suitable model for uncovering the physiological and pharmacological relevance of trace amine subtypes. In this regard, pilot studies indicate a 96% sequence identity for TAR1 in non-human primate and human. To establish fundamental information needed to explore TAR subtype function, we will investigate non-human primate TAR subtype structure, pharmacology, signal transduction and brain distribution. Aim 1 will determine whether human TAR subtypes (TAR1, 3, 4, 5) and structurally related orphan receptors (GPR57, GPR58 and PNR) exist in nonhuman primates. Based on these results, Aim 2 will utilize luciferase assays sensitive to different signal transduction pathways to uncover agonists as well as antagonists that block agonist-induced receptor activation. To characterize the pharmacological profile of these receptors, radioreceptor assays will be developed from lead compound(s) identified from luciferase assays. Aim 3 will map TAR subtype mRNA and protein distribution in primate brain using in situ hybridization, real-time RT-PCR and immunohistochemistry, to discern which receptor subtypes are expressed in brain for further exploration. Our pilot studies suggest that primate TARs are direct targets of psychostimulant drugs of abuse in brain. The proposed studies will form the basis for investigating the physiological and pharmacological relevance of trace amine receptors in a primate model, and may provide novel leads for developing therapeutic agents to treat addiction and possibly neuropsychiatric disorders.
